questions.prompt: According to the Catechism, human beings can know the existence of God with certainty by what means, even before receiving divine revelation?
choices: The natural light of human reason, from the created world
Only through the Bible
Only through a mystical experience
Only through the sacraments
questions.correctAnswer: The natural light of human reason, from the created world
questions.explanation: Echoing the First Vatican Council, the Catechism teaches that God, 'the first principle and last end of all things, can be known with certainty from the created world by the natural light of human reason' -- the starting point of natural theology.
questions.hint: Notice it says 'reason,' not 'faith' or 'revelation.'

citations.quote: God, the first principle and last end of all things, can be known with certainty from the created world by the natural light of human reason.
God, the source and end of all things, can be known with certainty from the consideration of created things, by the natural power of human reason

questions.prompt: True or False: The Catechism describes the desire for God as something implanted only in a few especially religious people, not in every human being.
questions.explanation: The Catechism teaches the opposite: 'The desire for God is written in the human heart, because man is created by God and for God' -- every person, not only the religious, is made with this orientation toward God.
questions.hint: This desire is written into human nature itself, not handed only to a spiritual elite.

citations.quote: The desire for God is written in the human heart, because man is created by God and for God; and God never ceases to draw man to himself.

questions.prompt: When Moses asked for God's name at the burning bush, God replied, 'I AM WHO I AM.' Catholic theology has long read this as revealing that God's very essence is:
choices: Existence itself -- Being, not merely a being among others
A secret name known only to priests
A title borrowed from a neighboring religion
A poetic way of avoiding the question
questions.correctAnswer: Existence itself -- Being, not merely a being among others
questions.explanation: Exodus 3:14 records God's self-revelation as 'I AM.' Catholic metaphysics, following Fathers like Augustine and theologians like Aquinas, reads this as revealing God not as one being among many, but as Being itself, the source of all that exists.
questions.hint: God didn't give a name like 'Bob' -- he described his own act of existing.

citations.quote: God replied to Moses: I am who I am. Then he added: This is what you will tell the Israelites: I AM has sent me to you.
Is Truth, therefore, nothing because it is neither diffused through space, finite, nor infinite? And You cried to me from afar, Yea, verily, 'I Am that I Am.'

questions.prompt: Pope St. John Paul II's encyclical Fides et Ratio opens by comparing faith and reason to two ____ on which the human spirit rises to contemplate truth.
questions.correctAnswer: wings
questions.explanation: The encyclical's famous opening line -- 'Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth' -- sets the tone for the whole document: faith and reason belong together, not at war.
questions.hint: Think of something a bird uses to fly, in pairs.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: True or False: The most basic law of reason, the principle of non-contradiction, states that the same thing cannot both be and not be true at the same time and in the same respect.
questions.explanation: Fides et Ratio affirms this and similar first principles as self-evident starting points reason cannot coherently deny -- without them, no reasoning, including theological reasoning, could get off the ground.
questions.hint: It can't be raining and not-raining, in the same place, at the same moment.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: Philosophers distinguish a creature's 'essence' (what it is) from its 'existence' (that it is). In God alone, Catholic metaphysics holds that these two are:
choices: Identical -- God's essence simply is to exist
Completely unrelated to one another
Both created by a higher being
Both illusions
questions.correctAnswer: Identical -- God's essence simply is to exist
questions.explanation: A creature could fail to exist without contradiction -- its essence doesn't require existence. God's essence, by contrast, simply is 'to exist': he cannot not be, which is part of what 'I AM WHO I AM' reveals.
questions.hint: Everything else could have not existed. This one being could not.

citations.quote: The revelation of the ineffable name 'I AM WHO AM' contains then the truth that God alone IS.

questions.prompt: Metaphysics asks a question the empirical sciences do not. Which?
choices: Not how things behave, but what it is for anything to exist at all
How accurately instruments can measure natural processes
Which religious claims are historically attested
How human beings ought to act
questions.correctAnswer: Not how things behave, but what it is for anything to exist at all
questions.explanation: The sciences describe how things within the world behave. Metaphysics asks what being itself is — a question no measurement can settle, because any measurement already presupposes something there to measure.
questions.hint: One of these questions is presupposed by every experiment rather than answered by one.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)

questions.prompt: True or False: When we call God good or wise, the words mean exactly what they mean when applied to a human being.
questions.explanation: False. Such words are used analogically: they say something genuinely true of God, but not in the same mode. Between Creator and creature no likeness can be noted without a greater unlikeness. Insisting the words mean exactly the same thing produces a God who is a very large creature; insisting they mean nothing produces silence.
questions.hint: There are three possibilities — same meaning, unrelated meaning, and something between. Only one is right.

questions.prompt: Classical theology says God is not one being among many but Being ____ — existence in itself, not a thing that happens to exist.
questions.correctAnswer: itself
questions.explanation: This is why God cannot be counted alongside creatures as one more item in an inventory. Asking whether the universe contains God, the way it contains galaxies, misunderstands the claim: the question is about the source of there being anything at all.
questions.hint: The claim is not that God is the greatest existing thing, but something stronger about existence.

questions.prompt: Match each foundational term to what it names.

pairs.right: What a thing is
That a thing is
Nothing can both be and not be in the same respect at once
Words said truly of God, but not in a creaturely mode

questions.explanation: These four recur throughout the topic. The essence/existence pair is the one to hold onto: in every creature they are distinct, which is why nothing in the world explains its own existence.
questions.hint: Two of these are a matched pair answering 'what' and 'whether'.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)

questions.prompt: The classical philosophical distinction between 'act' (what a thing actually is) and 'potency' (what a thing could become) primarily explains:
choices: How change is possible without a thing becoming a completely different substance
How to calculate the age of the universe
Which sacraments are valid
How many angels exist
questions.correctAnswer: How change is possible without a thing becoming a completely different substance
questions.explanation: A green apple has the potency to become red; when it does, the same apple persists through the change, moving from potentially red to actually red. Act and potency explain how one thing can genuinely change while remaining itself.
questions.hint: This distinction is about change over time, not about creation from nothing.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: True or False: In Thomistic metaphysics, 'pure act' -- actuality with no unrealized potency at all -- describes God alone.
questions.explanation: Every creature retains unrealized potential -- it could be otherwise than it currently is. God alone has no unrealized potential whatsoever: he simply and fully is, which is part of what it means to say his essence is to exist.
questions.hint: Everything else could still change into something it isn't yet. This one being cannot.

citations.quote: God replied to Moses: I am who I am. Then he added: This is what you will tell the Israelites: I AM has sent me to you.

questions.prompt: Because a creature is not pure act, it always retains some unrealized ____ -- some way it could be otherwise than it currently is.
questions.correctAnswer: potency
questions.explanation: A seated man has the potency to stand; a cold cup of coffee has the potency to warm up. Every creature, unlike God, is a mix of actuality and unrealized potential.
questions.hint: It's the opposite of 'act' in this classical pairing.

citations.quote: God replied to Moses: I am who I am. Then he added: This is what you will tell the Israelites: I AM has sent me to you.

questions.prompt: In classical metaphysics, an acorn has the potency to become an oak tree. This means the oak tree, before it grows, is:
choices: Not yet actual, but really possible given the acorn's own nature
Already fully actual, just hidden from view
Impossible, since acorns and oaks are unrelated
A different substance from the acorn entirely
questions.correctAnswer: Not yet actual, but really possible given the acorn's own nature
questions.explanation: Potency isn't mere logical possibility -- an acorn has the real, built-in potency to become an oak specifically, rooted in what an acorn already is by nature, not an arbitrary open-ended possibility.
questions.hint: The acorn's potency points toward one specific outcome, not just any outcome.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: True or False: 'Act,' in this philosophical sense, simply means 'a good deed,' unrelated to what a thing actually is.
questions.explanation: Here 'act' (from the Latin actus) means actuality or realization -- a thing's being fully what it is -- not a moral action. It's easy to confuse the philosophical term with the everyday English word.
questions.hint: This is a technical philosophical term, borrowed but not identical to the everyday word.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning in classical act/potency metaphysics.

pairs.right: What a thing actually is or actually has
What a thing could become or could have, but does not yet
Actuality with no unrealized potency at all -- God alone
The passage from potency to act

questions.explanation: Together these four terms form the backbone of the classical account of change: things move from what they could be to what they actually are, except God, who simply and fully is.
questions.hint: One of these four describes God uniquely; the others apply to any changing creature.

citations.quote: God replied to Moses: I am who I am. Then he added: This is what you will tell the Israelites: I AM has sent me to you.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: Why does change require something that persists through it?
choices: Otherwise there is no change but simple replacement — one thing ceasing and another beginning, with nothing that became different
Because all change is gradual
Because matter cannot be destroyed
Because time flows continuously
questions.correctAnswer: Otherwise there is no change but simple replacement — one thing ceasing and another beginning, with nothing that became different
questions.explanation: For a leaf to change from green to brown, the leaf must still be there to have changed. A subject persisting in potency, receiving a new act, is what distinguishes change from annihilation followed by creation.
questions.hint: Ask what would be missing if nothing carried over from before to after.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)

questions.prompt: True or False: Because God is pure act with no unrealised potency, classical theology concludes God cannot change.
questions.explanation: True, and the reasoning is worth following rather than memorising. To change is to move from potency to act. Something with no unrealised potency has nowhere to move — not because God is frozen or inert, but because there is no unrealised fullness for him to acquire.
questions.hint: Change means acquiring something not yet possessed. Ask what is left to acquire.

questions.prompt: A thing's potency is not nothing, but neither is it actual: the oak is really in the acorn as a genuine ____, not merely as someone's prediction.
questions.correctAnswer: potency
questions.explanation: Potency is a real feature of a thing, midway between actuality and sheer nothingness. An acorn can become an oak and a stone cannot, and that difference is in the acorn now — which is why potency cannot be reduced to what an observer expects.
questions.hint: The difference between an acorn and a stone is real before either becomes anything.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)

questions.prompt: Match each example to what it illustrates.

pairs.left: An acorn that could become an oak
pairs.right: Potency — a real capacity not yet realised

pairs.left: A grown oak standing in a field
pairs.right: Act — a capacity actually realised
No unrealised capacity, therefore no change

pairs.left: A stone that cannot become an oak
pairs.right: The absence of that potency, showing potency is real

questions.explanation: The last pairing carries the argument. If potency were merely a way of talking about expectations, there would be no difference between an acorn and a stone — and there plainly is.
questions.hint: One of these four is included to show that potency is not just a figure of speech.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)

questions.prompt: Aquinas' 'argument from motion,' the First Way, reasons that whatever is in motion or change is put into that motion by:
choices: Another, since nothing can move itself from potency to act in the very same respect
Pure chance, with no explanation needed
Its own future self, reaching backward in time
The observer watching it
questions.correctAnswer: Another, since nothing can move itself from potency to act in the very same respect
questions.explanation: A cold cup of coffee cannot make itself hot; something already hot (or actively heating) must act on it. Aquinas argues that tracing this chain of movers points, ultimately, to an unmoved mover -- what believers call God.
questions.hint: Can a potentially-hot cup of coffee heat itself, with nothing else acting on it?

citations.quote: The world, and man, attest that they contain within themselves neither their first principle nor their final end, but rather that they participate in Being itself, which alone is without origin or end.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: True or False: Aristotle and Aquinas distinguish four kinds of causes -- material, formal, efficient, and final -- that together explain why a thing is what it is.
questions.explanation: For a bronze statue: the bronze is the material cause, its particular shape is the formal cause, the sculptor is the efficient cause, and the purpose it's made for is the final cause. All four answer a different 'why' about the same statue.
questions.hint: Think of a statue: what it's made of, its shape, who made it, and what it's for.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: A thing's 'final cause' is the purpose or end toward which it is directed; Aquinas' Fifth Way argues from this order and purpose found throughout nature to the existence of an intelligent ____.
questions.correctAnswer: God
questions.explanation: Even non-intelligent things in nature consistently act toward ends -- an acorn toward becoming an oak, an eye toward seeing. Aquinas argues this built-in directedness points to an intelligence ordering it all.
questions.hint: Something has to be doing the directing, if the world consistently points toward ends.

citations.quote: Ever since the creation of the world, his invisible attributes of eternal power and divinity have been able to be understood and perceived in what he has made. As a result, they have no excuse

questions.prompt: In the classical four causes, the 'efficient cause' of a bronze statue is:
choices: The sculptor, who actively brings it into being
The bronze it's made of
The particular shape it takes
The reason it was commissioned
questions.correctAnswer: The sculptor, who actively brings it into being
questions.explanation: The efficient cause is the agent that actively produces the effect -- distinct from the material it's made of (material cause), the shape it takes (formal cause), and the purpose behind it (final cause).
questions.hint: This is the 'who' or 'what' that does the actual making.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: True or False: The principle of causality holds that everything that begins to exist must have a cause -- nothing simply pops into being uncaused.
questions.explanation: This principle underlies much of natural theology's reasoning toward God: a universe of things that begin to exist points beyond itself to something that does not begin to exist and needs no cause outside itself.
questions.hint: This is one of the 'first principles' Fides et Ratio treats as reason's bedrock.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: Match each of Aristotle's four causes to what it explains about a bronze statue.

pairs.right: The bronze it's made of
The particular shape or design it takes
The sculptor who makes it
The purpose it's made for

questions.explanation: A complete explanation of any changing thing, Aristotle held, answers all four 'whys' at once -- what it's made of, what shape it has, who or what produced it, and what it's for.
questions.hint: Four different questions you could ask about the same statue.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: Aquinas' First Way concerns a causal series ordered 'per se' rather than 'per accidens'. What is the difference?
choices: In a per se series the members depend on the first simultaneously, here and now; in a per accidens series each merely precedes the next in time
A per se series is longer than a per accidens series
A per se series concerns living things only
There is no real difference between them
questions.correctAnswer: In a per se series the members depend on the first simultaneously, here and now; in a per accidens series each merely precedes the next in time
questions.explanation: A hand moves a stick which moves a stone: remove the hand and the whole series stops at once. A father begets a son who begets a grandson: the grandfather can die and the series continues. The argument concerns the first kind, which is why 'but who caused God' and 'the universe could be infinitely old' both miss it.
questions.hint: One series collapses instantly if the first member is removed; the other does not.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)

questions.prompt: True or False: Aquinas' arguments require that the universe had a beginning in time.
questions.explanation: False, and Aquinas says so explicitly. He held the world's temporal beginning is known by faith, not demonstrated by reason, and he framed his arguments so they would work even on the assumption of an eternal universe. The dependence at issue is present-tense, not first in a sequence.
questions.hint: Ask whether a universe with no beginning would still need something to sustain it now.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)

questions.prompt: The ____ cause of a bronze statue is the shape or pattern that makes this bronze a statue rather than a lump.
questions.correctAnswer: formal
questions.explanation: Material and formal causes answer different questions about the same object: what it is made of, and what makes it this rather than merely that stuff. Modern usage has narrowed 'cause' to the efficient cause alone, which is why the fourfold scheme sounds strange at first.
questions.hint: Of the four causes, this one concerns the pattern rather than the stuff, the maker, or the purpose.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)

questions.prompt: Match each objection to a causal argument with what it misses.

pairs.right: The argument concludes to something whose existence is not received
A per se series concerns present dependence, not temporal order
It asks a different question — how things behave, not why anything is
An infinite per se series still explains nothing without a first member

questions.explanation: All four objections treat the argument as being about a very long chain of events in time. It is not; it is about what sustains anything in being at this moment, which is why length is irrelevant to it.
questions.hint: Every one of these reads the argument as a claim about history.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)

questions.prompt: The 'transcendentals' in classical metaphysics are properties said to belong to every single being simply because it exists. Which of the following is traditionally listed as a transcendental?
choices: Goodness
Color
Weight
Temperature
questions.correctAnswer: Goodness
questions.explanation: Being, Unity, Truth, Goodness, and (often) Beauty are the classical transcendentals -- properties that apply to absolutely everything that exists, unlike color or weight, which only some beings have.
questions.hint: The other three options only apply to physical objects, not to every kind of being.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: True or False: The medieval axiom 'omne ens est unum, verum, bonum' ('every being is one, true, good') expresses the doctrine of the transcendentals.
questions.explanation: This axiom summarizes the claim that unity, truth, and goodness aren't extra add-ons to being -- they're convertible with being itself. Wherever there is a being at all, these properties follow automatically.
questions.hint: This Latin phrase is basically a one-line summary of the whole doctrine.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: Because Being, Unity, Truth, and Goodness are 'convertible' with one another in classical metaphysics, whatever is fully real is, in due proportion, also fully intelligible and ____.
questions.correctAnswer: good
questions.explanation: 'Convertible' means these terms all pick out the same underlying reality from different angles -- so a fuller degree of being brings with it a fuller degree of unity, truth, and goodness, not separate, unrelated properties.
questions.hint: It's one of the transcendentals already named earlier in the sentence -- the moral one.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: Classical metaphysics regularly adds 'Beauty' to the shorter list of transcendentals (Being, Unity, Truth, Goodness). This reflects the conviction that beauty is:
choices: A real property of being itself, not merely a matter of subjective taste
Purely a modern invention with no basis in older philosophy
Identical to pleasure and nothing more
Irrelevant to theology
questions.correctAnswer: A real property of being itself, not merely a matter of subjective taste
questions.explanation: On this view, beauty is the splendor of a being's own truth and goodness, radiating outward and delighting the one who perceives it -- not simply whatever any individual happens to like.
questions.hint: The classical view resists reducing beauty to 'just personal opinion.'

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: True or False: In classical metaphysics, 'evil' is understood as a real, positive substance created alongside goodness, roughly equal and opposite to it.
questions.explanation: Following St. Augustine's mature rejection of Manichean dualism, the Church holds that evil is a privation -- a lack of a good that ought to be present -- not a positive thing God created. Everything God made, as such, is good.
questions.hint: Genesis says everything God made was good -- so where would a second, evil substance come from?

citations.quote: God looked at everything he had made, and found it very good.

questions.prompt: Match each transcendental to its basic meaning.

pairs.right: That a thing exists at all
That a thing is undivided in itself
That a thing is intelligible, knowable as it is
That a thing is desirable, complete according to its own nature

questions.explanation: Each transcendental highlights a different facet of the very same reality: to exist at all is already to be one, knowable, and desirable in some measure.
questions.hint: One is about existing, one about wholeness, one about being knowable, one about being desirable.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: Classical metaphysics defines truth as the conformity of intellect and thing. What follows about the world?
choices: Things are intelligible in themselves, so knowledge is a mind conforming to what is really there rather than imposing order on it
Truth is whatever a community agrees on
Truth exists only in propositions, never in things
The mind creates the order it finds
questions.correctAnswer: Things are intelligible in themselves, so knowledge is a mind conforming to what is really there rather than imposing order on it
questions.explanation: If truth is conformity, then things must have a nature to conform to. This is why the transcendental of truth is a claim about being before it is a claim about statements — the world is knowable because it is intelligible, not merely because we are clever.
questions.hint: Conformity requires two terms. Ask what the intellect is conforming to.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)

questions.prompt: True or False: Because goodness is convertible with being, anything that exists is good insofar as it exists.
questions.explanation: True, and it has a sharp consequence: nothing that exists is evil in its very being. A corrupt thing is a good thing lacking a good it should have — which is exactly the privation account, arrived at from the transcendentals rather than from Genesis.
questions.hint: If this is true, ask what is left for evil to be.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)

questions.prompt: Why are the transcendentals said to be 'convertible' with being rather than being species of it?
choices: They are not kinds of being but being itself considered under different aspects, so they add nothing to it and exclude nothing
They are the four highest categories of things that exist
They can be exchanged for one another in argument
They apply only to spiritual beings
questions.correctAnswer: They are not kinds of being but being itself considered under different aspects, so they add nothing to it and exclude nothing
questions.explanation: Unity, truth and goodness do not divide being into classes the way species divide a genus. They name the same reality regarded as undivided, as knowable, and as desirable — which is why every being has all of them rather than some being true and others good.
questions.hint: They do not carve being into parts. Ask what else they could be doing.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)

questions.prompt: Match each transcendental to the aspect of being it names.

pairs.right: Being as undivided in itself
Being as knowable to an intellect
Being as desirable to a will
Being as pleasing when perceived

questions.explanation: Truth and goodness are relational: they name being as it stands toward a knower and toward a desirer. That is why a purely mind-independent account of truth, or of goodness, is harder to state than it first appears.
questions.hint: Two of these involve a relation to someone; two do not.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)

questions.prompt: Aquinas' 'Five Ways' are five philosophical arguments for:
choices: The existence of God, reasoned from effects observable in the world
The number of angels in each choir
The date of Christ's return
The correct calendar for Easter
questions.correctAnswer: The existence of God, reasoned from effects observable in the world
questions.explanation: From motion, causation, contingency, degrees of perfection, and the order of nature, Aquinas argues that reason alone, reflecting on the world, can conclude that God exists -- prior to and apart from revelation.
questions.hint: Each of the five starts from something we can observe in the world around us.

citations.quote: converging and convincing arguments, which allow us to attain certainty about the truth
God, the source and end of all things, can be known with certainty from the consideration of created things, by the natural power of human reason

questions.prompt: True or False: The First Vatican Council solemnly taught that the existence of God cannot be known with certainty by reason alone, only by faith.
questions.explanation: Vatican I taught the opposite: God 'can be known with certainty from the created world by the natural light of human reason.' Faith is still needed to know the mysteries of the Trinity and Incarnation, but not for God's bare existence.
questions.hint: Vatican I's teaching runs the other direction from this statement.

citations.quote: God, the source and end of all things, can be known with certainty from the consideration of created things, by the natural power of human reason
God, the first principle and last end of all things, can be known with certainty from the created world by the natural light of human reason.

questions.prompt: Romans chapter 1 teaches that God's 'eternal power and divine nature' have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, through the things that have been ____.
questions.correctAnswer: made
questions.explanation: St. Paul argues that creation itself, rightly reasoned about, leaves people without excuse for failing to recognize God's existence -- a foundational scriptural basis for natural theology.
questions.hint: It's the created things themselves that reveal the Creator.

citations.quote: Ever since the creation of the world, his invisible attributes of eternal power and divinity have been able to be understood and perceived in what he has made. As a result, they have no excuse

questions.prompt: The 'argument from contingency' reasons that since everything in the world could have failed to exist (is contingent), there must ultimately be something that:
choices: Exists necessarily, not depending on anything else for its existence
Also could have failed to exist, just like everything else
Is the largest thing in the universe
Was created a very long time ago
questions.correctAnswer: Exists necessarily, not depending on anything else for its existence
questions.explanation: If every single thing merely could exist or not, an infinite chain of merely-possible things could never get started on its own. Something must exist necessarily, in itself, to ground the existence of everything contingent.
questions.hint: An endless chain of 'maybe it exists, maybe it doesn't' can't explain itself.

citations.quote: God, the source and end of all things, can be known with certainty from the consideration of created things, by the natural power of human reason

questions.prompt: True or False: Because natural theology can establish God's existence through reason alone, the Church considers divine revelation of mysteries like the Trinity and the Incarnation unnecessary.
questions.explanation: Reason can reach God's existence and some of his attributes, but the inner life of the Trinity and the Incarnation are truths reason could never discover on its own -- they depend entirely on God freely revealing himself.
questions.hint: Natural theology gets reason to God's doorstep -- it doesn't get inside the house on its own.

citations.quote: The Trinity is a mystery of faith in the strict sense, one of the 'mysteries that are hidden in God, which can never be known unless they are revealed by God'.

questions.prompt: Match each term in natural theology to its meaning.

pairs.right: Knowledge of God available to unaided human reason
Knowledge of God that depends on God's own self-disclosure
Aquinas' philosophical arguments for God's existence
Vatican I's teaching that God can be known with certainty by reason

questions.explanation: Natural and revealed theology are not competitors -- reason can establish that God exists and something of what he is like, while revelation alone discloses who God is in himself, as Trinity and as Christ Incarnate.
questions.hint: Two of these are broad categories of theology; two are specific arguments or documents.

citations.quote: God, the source and end of all things, can be known with certainty from the consideration of created things, by the natural power of human reason
God, the first principle and last end of all things, can be known with certainty from the created world by the natural light of human reason.

questions.prompt: What do the Five Ways actually conclude to, and what do they not?
choices: Each ends at something 'all call God' — an unmoved mover, a necessary being — not at the Trinity, which is known only by revelation
They demonstrate the Trinity philosophically
They prove the God of the Bible in every detail
They establish only that belief in God is permissible
questions.correctAnswer: Each ends at something 'all call God' — an unmoved mover, a necessary being — not at the Trinity, which is known only by revelation
questions.explanation: Overstating the conclusion is the commonest way these arguments are misused. They reach a first cause and no further; that this cause is Father, Son and Spirit is revealed, not deduced. Claiming more invites the fair reply that the arguments have not delivered it.
questions.hint: Ask what a purely philosophical argument could establish about a mystery known only by revelation.

questions.prompt: True or False: Since reason can reach God's existence, the Church holds that revelation about God is unnecessary.
questions.explanation: False, and Vatican I taught both halves. Reason can attain God's existence in principle; revelation remains morally necessary so that these truths can be known by everyone, readily, with firm certainty and without admixture of error. In principle attainable and in practice reliably attained are different claims.
questions.hint: Distinguish what reason can do in principle from what people actually manage without help.

questions.prompt: The argument from contingency reasons that if everything were contingent, there would be nothing now; so there must be something ____ — existing of itself.
questions.correctAnswer: necessary
questions.explanation: A contingent thing has existence received rather than owned. If every existing thing were like that, existence would have to come from somewhere else at every point and never actually be grounded. The argument is about a present dependency, not about a first event long ago.
questions.hint: The contrast term for contingent is not 'eternal' but something stronger.

questions.prompt: Match each claim in natural theology to its precise scope.

pairs.right: Taught by Vatican I as attainable in principle
So the truth is known by all, readily and without error
Conclude to a first cause, not to the Trinity
Two wings, neither reducible to the other

questions.explanation: The Church's position is a narrow path between rationalism, which makes revelation redundant, and fideism, which makes reason irrelevant. Dei Filius condemned both, and each of these four claims is doing work to hold that line.
questions.hint: Two of these guard against rationalism and two against fideism.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)

questions.prompt: God's self-revelation in Exodus 3:14, 'I AM WHO AM,' is read by Aquinas as revealing something unique about God's own being. What does it reveal?
choices: That in God alone, essence and existence are identical -- God does not merely possess existence, his very essence IS 'to exist'
That God's name is simply unknowable and has no philosophical content
That God is identical with the created universe
That existence is not really a coherent philosophical concept
questions.correctAnswer: That in God alone, essence and existence are identical -- God does not merely possess existence, his very essence IS 'to exist'
questions.explanation: Where every creature's essence (what it is) is really distinct from its existence (that it is) -- a human being's essence doesn't automatically guarantee that human being exists -- God's self-naming as 'I AM WHO AM' reveals that in God alone, essence and existence are identical: God's very essence simply is to exist, not a further property added to some prior 'what.'
questions.hint: Ask whether God's essence is something distinct from his existing, the way a creature's essence is distinct from whether it happens to exist.

citations.quote: God replied to Moses: I am who I am. Then he added: This is what you will tell the Israelites: I AM has sent me to you.

questions.prompt: Aquinas argues (De Ente et Essentia, ch. 4-5) that every creature's essence 'receives' an act of existing distinct from itself. What does this mean in practice?
choices: A creature's 'what it is' (its essence) does not by itself explain 'that it is' (its existence) -- existence must be received from an outside cause, since nothing in a creature's own essence guarantees it actually exists
A creature's essence and existence are simply two words for the same identical reality, with no real distinction at all
Only living creatures have an essence; non-living things have existence without any essence
This principle applies only to angels, not to physical creatures
questions.correctAnswer: A creature's 'what it is' (its essence) does not by itself explain 'that it is' (its existence) -- existence must be received from an outside cause, since nothing in a creature's own essence guarantees it actually exists
questions.explanation: Unlike God, whose essence simply is to exist, every creature's essence -- fully specifying what a horse or a human being is -- leaves entirely open whether that thing actually exists at all. Since essence alone cannot supply its own existence, existence must be received from an outside cause -- the basis of Aquinas's contingency argument for a first cause whose essence is existence itself.
questions.hint: Ask whether fully knowing what something is tells you, by itself, whether that thing actually exists.

citations.quote: The revelation of the ineffable name 'I AM WHO AM' contains then the truth that God alone IS.

questions.prompt: True or False: A tree's specific bark color is an example of its substantial form, while its being a tree at all (rather than a rock or an animal) is an example of an accidental form.
questions.explanation: This has the two terms reversed: the tree's substantial form is what makes it a tree at all -- what it fundamentally is, its 'treeness' -- while its bark color is an accidental form, a feature the tree could have differently (or lose) without ceasing to be a tree in the first place.
questions.hint: One of these two features could change without the thing ceasing to be what it fundamentally is; the other could not.

citations.quote: The unity of soul and body is so profound that one has to consider the soul to be the 'form' of the body

questions.prompt: Why, per hylomorphic theory, can 'prime matter' never exist on its own, entirely unformed?
choices: Prime matter is pure potentiality with no actuality of its own -- it only ever exists already actualized by some substantial form, never as a free-floating, formless 'stuff'
Prime matter is simply a synonym for empty space
Prime matter can exist on its own perfectly well, contrary to traditional hylomorphic theory
Prime matter only applies to non-physical, spiritual realities
questions.correctAnswer: Prime matter is pure potentiality with no actuality of its own -- it only ever exists already actualized by some substantial form, never as a free-floating, formless 'stuff'
questions.explanation: Prime matter names pure potentiality for taking on some substantial form -- by definition it has no actuality of its own apart from being actualized by a form. It never exists as a free-floating, undetermined 'stuff' waiting around; wherever matter exists in the world, it is always already the matter of some actually-existing, formed substance.
questions.hint: Prime matter is defined as pure potential -- and pure potential, by definition, needs something actual to actualize it.

citations.quote: The unity of soul and body is so profound that one has to consider the soul to be the 'form' of the body

questions.prompt: How does the essence/existence distinction help explain why the Church describes creation as a 'radical dependence' relation rather than a change or a making-from-some-preexisting-material?
choices: Since every creature's essence must continually receive its act of existing from outside itself, creation names the total, ongoing dependence of a creature's very existing on God, not a one-time change performed on some pre-existing stuff
Creation is simply a synonym for a chemical or physical transformation of matter already present
The essence/existence distinction has no bearing on the doctrine of creation at all
Creation means God is identical with the created world's own essence
questions.correctAnswer: Since every creature's essence must continually receive its act of existing from outside itself, creation names the total, ongoing dependence of a creature's very existing on God, not a one-time change performed on some pre-existing stuff
questions.explanation: Because a creature's essence never supplies its own existence, that existence must be continually received from God as its source -- creation, understood this way, is not a change (which presupposes something already existing that gets altered) but the total, radical dependence of a creature's very act of existing on God, at every moment it exists, not just at a first moment.
questions.hint: A 'change' presupposes something already existing to be changed -- creation, understood through esse/essentia, is more radical than that.

citations.quote: Nothing exists that does not owe its existence to God the Creator. The world began when God's word drew it out of nothingness.

questions.prompt: Match each term or claim from this level to its precise meaning.

pairs.right: That a thing actually is, distinct from what it is
What a thing is, which in creatures does not by itself guarantee that it exists

pairs.left: 'God's essence is His existence' (STh I q.3 a.4)
pairs.right: A substantive claim that God alone needs no outside cause to exist, unlike every creature
Pure potentiality, never existing except as already actualized by some substantial form

questions.explanation: Each of these terms deepens ground already touched at levels 1-2 (potential vs. actual, what makes a thing what it is) with the Church's and Aquinas's own precise technical vocabulary, wired to the specific argument each term does real work in.
questions.hint: Two of these terms form a single pair naming the same basic distinction, applied differently to God and to creatures.

citations.quote: The revelation of the ineffable name 'I AM WHO AM' contains then the truth that God alone IS.

questions.prompt: Divine simplicity holds that God has no parts. What does this rule out?
choices: Any composition in God — of matter and form, essence and existence, or substance and attribute; God does not HAVE goodness, he IS it
That God can be described in more than one way
That God knows individual creatures
That God acts in history
questions.correctAnswer: Any composition in God — of matter and form, essence and existence, or substance and attribute; God does not HAVE goodness, he IS it
questions.explanation: Anything composed depends on its parts and on whatever assembled them, so a composite God would be a caused God. Simplicity is why divine attributes are not components: they are the one divine reality named from our side in different ways.
questions.hint: Ask what a composite thing depends on, and whether that can be true of the first cause.

questions.prompt: True or False: Saying creation is a 'radical dependence' means the universe needed a push at the beginning and has run on its own since.
questions.explanation: False. On the essence/existence account, a creature does not own its existing; it receives it. What is received must go on being given, so creation is a present-tense relation of dependence rather than a past event. Withdraw the giving and there is not a ruin but nothing at all.
questions.hint: Ask whether existence is something a creature has once, or receives continuously.

questions.prompt: Why does hylomorphism say prime matter cannot exist on its own?
choices: Because to exist is to be something definite, and prime matter is pure potency with no form — so it is a principle of things, not a thing
Because it is too small to observe
Because God has not created it yet
Because it exists only inside stars
questions.correctAnswer: Because to exist is to be something definite, and prime matter is pure potency with no form — so it is a principle of things, not a thing
questions.explanation: Prime matter is what persists through substantial change, considered apart from any form it happens to have. Considered that way it is not stuff of a very basic kind; it is a principle we distinguish in thought, and asking where a lump of it is mistakes an analysis for an inventory.
questions.hint: Ask whether something with no form at all could be any particular thing.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it precisely denotes.

pairs.right: What makes a thing the kind of thing it is
A modification a thing can gain or lose while remaining itself
Pure potency, a principle rather than a thing
No composition in God of any kind

questions.explanation: The substantial/accidental distinction is the one that does daily work: a tree painted white is still a tree, a tree burned to ash is not. Everything hylomorphism says about the soul depends on getting that difference right first.
questions.hint: Two of these concern what a thing IS; one what it merely has; one concerns God.

questions.prompt: Hylomorphism teaches the human soul is the substantial form of the body -- one substance, not two things glued together. How does this differ from both Cartesian substance dualism and materialism?
choices: Unlike Cartesian dualism (two complete substances, mind and body, mysteriously interacting), and unlike materialism (only matter is real, with mind reducible to or illusory alongside it), hylomorphism holds a human being is a single substance whose form (the soul) actualizes its matter (the body) into one living, thinking whole
Hylomorphism agrees entirely with Cartesian dualism and simply adds new vocabulary for the same two-substance view
Hylomorphism agrees entirely with materialism that mind is nothing but brain activity, with no real distinct substantial form
Hylomorphism denies that human beings have bodies at all
questions.correctAnswer: Unlike Cartesian dualism (two complete substances, mind and body, mysteriously interacting), and unlike materialism (only matter is real, with mind reducible to or illusory alongside it), hylomorphism holds a human being is a single substance whose form (the soul) actualizes its matter (the body) into one living, thinking whole
questions.explanation: Aquinas's hylomorphism (ST I q.75-76) charts a genuine third position: not two separate substances awkwardly joined (Descartes's dualism), and not matter alone with mind eliminated or reduced away (materialism), but one single substance -- a human being -- whose substantial form (the soul) is what actualizes and organizes the matter (the body) into a single living, thinking whole.
questions.hint: The key move is 'one substance, not two,' but also 'a real form, not nothing but matter.'

citations.quote: The unity of soul and body is so profound that one has to consider the soul to be the 'form' of the body

questions.prompt: An objector says, 'Neuroscience shows thought simply reduces to brain states, so there's no need to posit a soul at all.' Using hylomorphism, what is the accurate response?
choices: Hylomorphism doesn't deny thought is closely correlated with and dependent on brain activity in this life -- it denies that the correlation by itself settles the deeper metaphysical question of what kind of thing is actually doing the thinking, which is a different question than neuroscience alone can answer
The Church denies any connection whatsoever between brain activity and thought
Hylomorphism requires denying that neuroscience has discovered anything real about brain function
This objection has no relevance to the soul-as-substantial-form claim at all
questions.correctAnswer: Hylomorphism doesn't deny thought is closely correlated with and dependent on brain activity in this life -- it denies that the correlation by itself settles the deeper metaphysical question of what kind of thing is actually doing the thinking, which is a different question than neuroscience alone can answer
questions.explanation: Hylomorphism happily accepts that thought is deeply dependent on and correlated with brain states in this embodied life -- the soul as substantial form actualizes a genuinely material body, after all. What it denies is that discovering this correlation, by itself, answers the further metaphysical question of what kind of underlying reality is actually doing the thinking -- a question neuroscience's own methods, which study correlations and mechanisms, are not positioned to settle on their own.
questions.hint: The accurate response accepts the neuroscience while distinguishing a different question the neuroscience alone doesn't answer.

citations.quote: The unity of soul and body is so profound that one has to consider the soul to be the 'form' of the body

questions.prompt: Aquinas argues (ST I q.75 a.2) that the human soul's capacity to know universal concepts (like 'triangle-in-general,' not just this one triangle) implies something important about the soul's own nature. What is it?
choices: The soul's own act of existing and operation is not wholly dependent on matter, since grasping a universal concept -- which applies to indefinitely many particular instances -- is not itself a purely material or bodily operation the way sensation is
The soul is a purely physical organ located in a specific part of the brain
Universal concepts do not actually exist and knowledge of them is an illusion
This capacity proves the soul has no real connection to the body whatsoever
questions.correctAnswer: The soul's own act of existing and operation is not wholly dependent on matter, since grasping a universal concept -- which applies to indefinitely many particular instances -- is not itself a purely material or bodily operation the way sensation is
questions.explanation: Sensation is always of a particular, material thing here and now; but grasping a universal concept ('triangle-in-general,' applying to indefinitely many actual and possible triangles) is not tied to any one particular material instance the way sensation is -- Aquinas takes this as evidence that the intellectual soul's own operation, and therefore its very act of existing, is not wholly dependent on matter, even though the soul is genuinely the form of a material body.
questions.hint: Compare grasping one particular triangle you're looking at right now to grasping the concept 'triangle' that fits any triangle whatsoever.

citations.quote: The Church teaches that every spiritual soul is created immediately by God - it is not 'produced' by the parents

questions.prompt: True or False: Per hylomorphic theory, a corpse immediately after death, despite having nearly identical matter to the living body that preceded it, is not actually the same kind of thing as that living body, because the substantial form (the soul) that had actualized that matter into a living human being is no longer present.
questions.explanation: Hylomorphism holds that a substance's identity comes from its substantial form actualizing its matter into a specific kind of thing -- when the soul, as substantial form, departs at death, the remaining matter is no longer actualized as a living human body but begins to be organized (or disorganized) as a corpse, a genuinely different kind of thing despite the near-identical matter at the moment of death.
questions.hint: The matter barely changes at the moment of death, but what actualizes that matter into a specific kind of thing does.

citations.quote: The Church teaches that every spiritual soul is created immediately by God - it is not 'produced' by the parents

questions.prompt: The phrase 'ghost in the machine' is sometimes used to caricature any view that posits a soul, imagining it as a separate spectral pilot secretly steering the body's machinery. Why does this caricature actually misdescribe hylomorphism specifically?
choices: Hylomorphism doesn't posit two separate things (a 'ghost' and a 'machine') interacting -- it holds the soul is the form of the body itself, meaning there is only one substance, a single living human being, not a pilot inside a separate vehicle
The caricature is actually an accurate description of exactly what hylomorphism teaches
Hylomorphism agrees the body is a machine with no substantial form at all
The phrase 'ghost in the machine' was coined by Aquinas himself to describe his own theory approvingly
questions.correctAnswer: Hylomorphism doesn't posit two separate things (a 'ghost' and a 'machine') interacting -- it holds the soul is the form of the body itself, meaning there is only one substance, a single living human being, not a pilot inside a separate vehicle
questions.explanation: The 'ghost in the machine' image (originally aimed at Cartesian dualism) pictures two separate things -- an immaterial pilot and a material vehicle -- interacting from the outside. Hylomorphism denies exactly this picture: the soul isn't a separate thing riding inside the body, but the body's own substantial form, meaning body and soul together constitute one single substance, not two interacting things.
questions.hint: The caricature assumes two separate things interacting -- hylomorphism's whole point is that there's only one thing.

citations.quote: The unity of soul and body is so profound that one has to consider the soul to be the 'form' of the body

questions.prompt: Match each position or objection to hylomorphism's precise response.

pairs.left: Cartesian substance dualism (two complete substances interacting)
pairs.right: Hylomorphism holds one substance, not two -- the soul is the body's own form, not a separate substance riding within it

pairs.left: Eliminative materialism (e.g., Paul Churchland's view that mental-state concepts will ultimately be eliminated in favor of purely neural description)
pairs.right: Hylomorphism accepts real dependence on brain states in this life, while denying that correlation alone settles what kind of thing is actually doing the thinking
Misdescribes hylomorphism as positing two separate interacting things, when it holds only one substance

pairs.left: The soul's grasp of universal concepts
pairs.right: Evidence the soul's own operation is not wholly dependent on matter, per ST I q.75 a.2

questions.explanation: Each of these responses engages a real, currently-held or historically influential position on its own terms, rather than a strawman -- the discipline this level requires before drafting any 'wrong answer' distractor.
questions.hint: Two of these are named philosophical positions; two are objections or evidence internal to the hylomorphic argument itself.

citations.quote: The unity of soul and body is so profound that one has to consider the soul to be the 'form' of the body

questions.prompt: An objector argues that since mental states correlate exactly with brain states, the mind just is the brain. What does hylomorphism reply?
choices: Correlation is exactly what it predicts — the soul is the form of THIS body, so of course thinking has a bodily aspect; correlation would refute a ghost-in-the-machine dualism, not this
The correlations are not real
The soul operates independently of the brain entirely
Neuroscience cannot study the mind at all
questions.correctAnswer: Correlation is exactly what it predicts — the soul is the form of THIS body, so of course thinking has a bodily aspect; correlation would refute a ghost-in-the-machine dualism, not this
questions.explanation: The objection lands on Descartes, not on Aquinas. If soul and body were two things loosely joined, tight correlation would be surprising. On the hylomorphic account they are one substance, and the finding is what the theory expects — which is why the argument has to be answered by asking which view it targets.
questions.hint: Ask which theory of the soul the objection would actually damage.

questions.prompt: How does the soul as substantial form bear on the resurrection of the body?
choices: Since the soul is the form of this body, the risen body is the same person's body — identity is secured by the form, not by tracking the original atoms
The risen body will be composed of the identical atoms as before
The resurrection concerns the soul only
Bodily identity cannot be maintained on this account
questions.correctAnswer: Since the soul is the form of this body, the risen body is the same person's body — identity is secured by the form, not by tracking the original atoms
questions.explanation: The atoms in a living body are replaced many times over a lifetime without anyone becoming a different person, so material continuity was never what identity rested on. The same principle answers the old objection about scattered or consumed remains.
questions.hint: You are not made of the same atoms you were as a child. Ask what made you the same person anyway.

questions.prompt: True or False: On the Catholic account, a human being is a soul that happens to be using a body.
questions.explanation: False, and the Church rejects this explicitly. The unity of body and soul is so profound that the soul is called the form of the body — one nature, not a pilot in a vessel. This is why the body is destined for resurrection rather than discarded, and why despising the body is a Gnostic instinct rather than a Christian one.
questions.hint: Ask whether this description would make the resurrection of the body necessary or pointless.

questions.prompt: Match each position on soul and body to what hylomorphism says about it.

pairs.right: Two substances joined; makes their interaction a mystery
One substance, but denies the reality of mind
One substance, form and matter, neither reducible to the other
A caricature of dualism, not a description of this view

questions.explanation: Hylomorphism is regularly attacked as though it were the first position and defended as though it were the second. Naming what it is not is most of the work of stating what it is.
questions.hint: Two of these are rival theories, one is the Catholic account, and one is a caricature.
